title: What the Museum Left Off Its Labels
body:
When the city museum reopened its maritime gallery last spring, most visitors noticed the new lighting before they noticed the labels; had the lighting been left alone, they would have seen at once that the labels were the real change. For decades the ships had been described as triumphs of engineering, and the sailors who crewed them were mentioned only in passing. The curators have rewritten almost every caption, however, and the result is a gallery that tells an uncomfortable story with remarkable restraint.

Had the museum added a modest panel on working conditions, few people would have objected. Instead, the curators decided to rethink the whole narrative, which inevitably drew criticism from donors who had funded the original displays. Several of them have argued that the new captions are overly political, although the wording is strikingly measured. A model of a nineteenth-century clipper, for instance, is now accompanied by an extract from a deckhand's diary describing the hunger that set in after the ship was becalmed for three weeks.

The decision was not taken lightly. The curators have spent two years consulting historians, descendants of sailors and, crucially, the volunteers who guide school groups through the rooms every morning. If they had skipped that consultation, the gallery would have lost the trust of the very people who explain it to the public. Nevertheless, the museum has paid a price: a long-standing sponsor withdrew its support in the summer, and the funding gap has not yet been closed. Whether the gamble pays off will depend on whether visitors bother to read the labels at all, which is precisely the question the next annual report is expected to answer.
